job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here are the issues, in section order. Some, such as the grandfathering in Sec. 3(b), may be deliberate policy choices. I've listed them anyway because they affect who the bill actually reaches. I can't see the pre-amendment text, so I can't tell which problems the October 6 manager's amendment introduced. The legal-risk points (vagueness, nondelegation, retroactivity) are flags for counsel, not conclusions.

**Definitions (Sec. 2)**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "single vessel" threshold.** The 10,000-ton line is measured per vessel, with no rule aggregating a fleet, a coordinated operation, or affiliated companies. Splitting is probably uneconomic at true commercial scale, but it matters for pilot and test operations near the line.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), how the threshold is measured.** The text doesn't say whether tonnage is wet or dry weight (nodules carry significant moisture) or where it's measured (seabed, deck, or landing). "Per year" is also undefined (calendar year or rolling 12 months), so partial-year operations are ambiguous.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "other mineral resources."** Neither term is defined, so it's unclear whether lifting, collecting, or onboard processing counts, or whether sulfides, crusts, and sediments are included. The phrase could also be read broadly enough to catch offshore oil and gas or sand and gravel dredging, which invites challenge and unintended opposition.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), the 200-meter depth and no geographic scope.** 200 meters is roughly the continental shelf edge, not the deep ocean, and the bill never says whether it covers the U.S. EEZ and shelf, areas beyond national jurisdiction, or both. It also doesn't say how depth is measured when a collector crosses depth contours.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B) and Sec. 6, undefined "Secretary."** Sec. 2 never defines "the Secretary," and Sec. 6 refers to the Secretary of State, so a reader could take the Sec. 2(1)(B) authority to mean State. The responsible agency (presumably Commerce/NOAA) needs to be named.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), standardless catch-all.** "Risks… comparable" has no criteria, no rulemaking or notice requirement, and no statement of whether the determination must precede the conduct. Because a Sec. 3 violation can turn on it and Sec. 5(b) is criminal, this is the most obvious vagueness and nondelegation target.

7. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person."** The definition omits foreign-organized subsidiaries of U.S. companies, LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and permanent residents, and "State" may not cover D.C. or the territories. There is no ownership or control test, so a foreign subsidiary or joint venture can sit outside Sec. 3(a).

8. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel."** A vessel under 5,000 gross tons can still recover more than 10,000 tons yet escape the registry. The "equipped for" test can also be dodged with modular or leased equipment, separate support or shuttle vessels, or non-vessel platforms, and no tonnage measurement convention is specified.

**Prohibition (Sec. 3)**

9. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States."** The phrase is undefined, so it's unclear whether it covers the territorial sea, EEZ, or shelf, or foreign-flag vessels in U.S. waters or ports. Foreign persons mining outside U.S. waters aren't reached at all.

10. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in" only.** Financing, insuring, supplying, transporting, processing, importing, and selling seabed minerals aren't prohibited. Reaching those actors would depend on general aiding or conspiracy law.

11. **Sec. 3, no relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend, repeal, or override NOAA's existing licensing and permitting authority for deep seabed minerals (the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, which is worth confirming with counsel) or any other statute. A permit holder could argue conflict or reliance, and it's unclear which law controls.

12. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license" undefined.** The text doesn't say who must have issued it. A foreign-government or International Seabed Authority-type contract might qualify.

13. **Sec. 3(b), exempts "mining," not exploration.** A licensee can apparently conduct full commercial-scale recovery, with no cap on volume or area, because the exemption removes the activity from Sec. 3(a) entirely.

14. **Sec. 3(b), no limits or conditions.** Nothing addresses transfer, renewal, amendment, area expansion, or loss of the exemption if the license is suspended or revoked. It also creates an incentive to rush licenses through before enactment.

15. **Sec. 3(c), "environmental assessment."** The term is undefined and purpose-based, with no cap on volume, duration, or area, no government approval, no bar on selling recovered material, and no reporting. Test mining or bulk sampling could be framed as assessment, and a subjective purpose is hard to disprove.

**Registry (Sec. 4)**

16. **Sec. 4(a), "operator" and registration mechanics.** "Operator" is undefined (owner, charterer, or manager?), and there's no deadline, content requirement, or rulemaking authority for NOAA. Nothing says whether foreign-flag or foreign-operated vessels must register or what jurisdictional hook applies.

17. **Sec. 4, no enforcement.** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report has no penalty in the Act. The duty to report also applies only to "registered" operators, so an operator that never registers has no reporting duty.

18. **Sec. 4(b), reports can't verify anything.** The report must only "describe" recovery activities. There are no required data (tonnage, location, depth, dates), no certification standard, no recordkeeping, no audit, inspection, or vessel-tracking authority, and no due dates for "quarterly." NOAA would have little ability to detect a 10,000-ton crossing.

**Penalties (Sec. 5)**

19. **Sec. 5(a) vs. Sec. 8, date conflict.** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. It's unclear whether conduct in that window is a violation, and a reading that penalizes it invites fair-notice and retroactivity challenges.

20. **Sec. 5(a), no enforcement machinery.** No agency is designated to assess or collect penalties, and there's no hearing process, no assessment factors, and no injunctive relief. There is also no seizure or forfeiture of vessels or cargo, no boarding or inspection authority, no inflation adjustment, and no authorization of appropriations.

21. **Sec. 5(a), deterrence.** A cap of $1 million per day, with no floor and no disgorgement, could be modest against the revenue of a commercial-scale operation, which is worth checking against industry figures. "Each day on which the violation occurs" also doesn't address continuous or multi-day operations.

22. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully."** The text doesn't say whether the defendant must know of the prohibition, the threshold, or a Sec. 2(1)(B) determination. Imprisonment reaches only individuals, there's no officer-liability provision, and venue for high-seas conduct isn't addressed (confirm whether the general high-seas venue statute fills the gap).

**International agreement (Sec. 6)**

23. **Sec. 6, unclear and unenforceable.** "Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" could set a deadline for starting talks or for concluding them. "Equivalent" is undefined, and there's no reporting requirement, consequence, or link to existing international regimes. Until then, foreign competitors face no restriction.

**Duration (Sec. 7)**

24. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b), direct conflict.** Sec. 7(a) keeps the prohibition in place until Congress acts, while Sec. 7(b) ends the whole Act after 10 years regardless. As written, 7(a) works only as an early-exit route.

25. **Sec. 7(a), undefined mechanism.** Nothing requires, funds, or sets a timeline for the National Academies report, and "serious harm" is undefined. A joint resolution that "finds" doesn't say the prohibition ends on enactment, and the resolution is subject to a presidential veto with no expedited procedures.

26. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause.** It's unclear whether pending enforcement actions and penalties for pre-sunset violations survive, and whether the general federal savings statute is enough. The 10 years also run from enactment, so the prohibition is operative for only about 9.5 years, and operators can plan to wait it out.

**Effective date (Sec. 8)**

27. **Sec. 8, 180-day gap.** Operators can expand activity, stockpile, and build reliance or takings arguments with no interim restrictions. The Sec. 6 and Sec. 7(b) clocks run from enactment while the prohibition runs from the effective date, and there's no registration deadline.

**Cross-cutting**

28. **No lead agency or rulemaking authority.** Apart from NOAA's registry role, no agency is assigned to implement, interpret, or enforce the Act. That compounds items 5, 16, 18, and 20.

29. **No severability clause.** A successful challenge to one provision, such as the Sec. 2(1)(B) catch-all, could put the whole Act at risk.

30. **Undefined terms.** "Person," "State," "seabed," "vessel," "mining," "serious harm," and "environmental assessment" are all used without definitions. Several of these are the hinge words for the exemptions and penalties.

If it would help for the newsletter or markup preview, I can sort these into tiers (largest loopholes, enforcement gaps, litigation risks) or draft a short plain-language explainer of the top five.
